# Diagnosing the 2011 Jeep Compass No-Start and P0688 Code

When a 2011 Jeep Compass presents with an engine crank-no-start condition, the initial data often points directly to the Totally Integrated Power Module (TIPM). In this specific case, scanning the vehicle reveals a stored DTC P0688: ASD Relay Control Sense. While the code suggests a communication or signal issue within the anti-theft/security domain, the physical symptoms tell a different story about power distribution.

The diagnostic process begins by verifying the complaint and reading the codes. Once P0688 is confirmed, the investigation shifts to the TIPM fuse block located under the hood. A standard multimeter check reveals that fuses 23 and 26 are dead, showing zero voltage on both sides. It is critical here to distinguish between a blown internal fuse element and an upstream power loss. In this scenario, visual inspection of the fusible links—specifically those feeding into these circuits—shows they remain intact. This observation narrows the scope significantly: if the primary fusible links are good, the issue lies either in the TIPM's internal relay logic or a broken circuit between the battery and the module itself.

Understanding the relationship between P0688 and the lack of power on fuses 23 and 26 is key to solving the no-start. The ASD (Automatic Shutdown) relay controls fuel pump operation and ignition timing. When the TIPM fails to energize the ASD relay properly, or if it detects a voltage spike that triggers its internal protection logic, it may cut power to downstream fuses like 23 and 26 as a safety measure.

From an engineering perspective, this behavior mimics a fail-safe state. The TIPM monitors the "Control Sense" line; if the signal is erratic or absent due to a shorted coil or wiring harness issue, the module defaults to locking out high-current outputs to prevent fire hazards or further damage. This explains why you see no voltage at the fuse terminals even though the fusible links are fine—the module has internally disconnected the circuit.

To troubleshoot this without immediately replacing the TIPM—a costly and often frustrating part swap—engineers should consider bench testing or isolating the input side. If the battery voltage is confirmed good at the main positive terminal of the TIPM, the suspect components narrow down to the internal ASD relay contacts or the sense circuitry itself. However, one must be cautious about interpreting fuse status alone. A lack of power on fuses 23 and 26 does not automatically confirm a bad TIPM; it confirms a loss of distribution that *could* stem from the module's protective logic.

In modern automotive systems like this Jeep platform, software updates can sometimes alter how these sensors interact with the relay control. While hardware faults are common on high-mileage units, verifying the input signal integrity before condemning the module is a necessary step. If the TIPM has suffered internal corrosion or contact welding on the ASD relay, it will fail to close the circuit, resulting in no fuel delivery and the specific fuse drop observed here.

The final verification often involves checking for continuity from the battery positive to the TIPM input terminals with the key off, ensuring no open wires exist before blaming the module. Once power integrity is confirmed at the input, replacing the TIPM usually restores function, as these modules frequently fail internally after years of thermal cycling and high current loads.
